title: The Lehrhaus Runs Backwards
hookLine: Rosenzweig's house of learning began from adults' lives and moved toward the text
carry: learning runs from your life back to the torah
tomorrow: why keep teaching when your students can't leave the camp?

lines: DESCRIBE A TRADITION THAT SHAPED YOU.
cards: The essay prompt on Noa's screen says: describe a tradition that has shaped you. She stares at it. She knows the Shabbat songs, a few stories, her grandfather's soup ladle.

She doesn't feel like she knows enough Torah to write a word. Rosenzweig would have said she's starting in exactly the right place. In Frankfurt he opened a house of learning for adults, the Lehrhaus.
And he said its learning had to run in reverse order.

teach.h: THE OLD WAY: TEXT INTO LIFE.
teach.b: In his opening address, Rosenzweig described the old way. A child grew up inside the text, and learning flowed out from the Torah into life. But the adults walking into his Lehrhaus had grown up far from that.
Their lives were full of other things: work, science, art, cities. So he turned the direction around.

Start from the edge, from life as you're living it, and travel back toward the center, the text. Nobody had to pretend to be closer than they were. The questions people brought from home and work were the doorway.
The Torah has a line that sounds like his permission slip: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Near, not across an ocean.
So for Noa the answer isn't to memorize something impressive by Friday.
Start with the ladle, the packing, the move. Ask what it's about.

teach.h: LEARNING RUNS FROM YOUR LIFE BACK TO THE TORAH.
teach.b: Then go looking for the text that has already asked it. That's the thing to repeat tonight: Rosenzweig didn't lower the bar. He moved the starting line to where people actually stand.

how: Some adult Jewish learning programs draw on Rosenzweig's Lehrhaus model, inviting people to bring questions from their own lives to the study of Jewish texts.

games.q: what does “from life to text” mean?
o: starting study from your own life and traveling toward the Torah
turning the stories of the Torah into plays for a stage
copying a holy book out by hand to learn it by heart

games.q: learning in reverse — tap the pairs.
p: from the Torah out into life
from life back toward the text
the word is very nigh unto thee

s: Rosenzweig's Lehrhaus began with the text and worked outward
he said its learning ran in reverse: from life toward the text.
Deuteronomy says the word is near, in your mouth and heart
Rosenzweig lowered the bar so adults wouldn't need the text
he moved the starting point; the journey still ends at the text.

games.q: your uncle, who hasn't opened a Jewish book in decades, asks your book club what he could possibly bring. what's the Lehrhaus answer?
o: bring a question from his own life; the club will look for the text that asks it.
read the commentaries first, so he isn't behind everyone else.
just listen for a year until he knows enough to speak.
games.why: Rosenzweig started from life as people lived it and traveled back toward the text.

practice: Name one question your week has handed you, about a move, a choice, a person.
Then make a small plan: what you want to understand, what usually stops you from looking, and one place you'll look first, a verse, a book or someone older than you.

wordCard.voice: From life to text: Rosenzweig's way of learning, starting from where adults actually live and traveling back toward the Torah.

orig.note: Hebrew: house of study. Rosenzweig's German Lehrhaus means house of learning.

carryVoice: Carry this: learning runs from your life back to the Torah. Your own week can be the first page you read.

sources.ref: Franz Rosenzweig, address at the opening of the Freies Jüdisches Lehrhaus, Frankfurt (learning in reverse order, from the periphery to the center)

sources.q: But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.
